Sixth grade science · Unit 5

Plate Tectonics & Rocks

The ground under your feet is a moving puzzle floating on slow-flowing rock. It built the Himalayas, shakes California, and made the stones in your driveway. Michigan's Great Lakes are the work of a one-mile-thick wall of ice. Let's see how it all fits together.

Where we left off: Unit 4 followed the Sun's energy through air and water. Earth has a second energy source: heat from deep inside. You may already have learned about convection, rising warm material and sinking cool material. The same idea, in very slow motion, moves the plates, and the forces from Unit 3 are what push, pull, and bend rock.

Concept 1 · Inside Earth

Earth has layers

Earth is built in layers: a thin crust, a thick flowing mantle, a liquid outer core, and a solid inner core. It gets hotter and more squeezed the deeper you go.

Analogy

A peach

Earth's crust is only about 0.5% of the way to the center: thinner relative to the planet than a peach skin is to the peach. Under it the mantle is a thick layer of hot rock that moves very slowly.

Where it breaks: a peach is solid all the way through. Earth's mantle flows like extremely thick syrup, and the core is mostly iron, not fruit.

Try it

Drill down

Data

Temperature climbs with depth

Approximate values. The deepest hole ever drilled (Kola, Russia) reached only 12 km, about 0.2% of the way to the center and already 180 °C.

Concept 2 · Moving plates

The ground is a slow puzzle

Earth's crust and top of the mantle break into plates that creep a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. They meet at three kinds of boundaries.

Analogy

Crackers on simmering oatmeal

Heat from below makes the oatmeal circulate in slow loops, and the crackers ride on top, jostle, and split. The mantle does the same thing to the plates, just far more slowly: convection, as in Unit 2.

Where it breaks: oatmeal is a pot of fluid; the mantle is solid rock that flows only over millions of years.

Diagram

Three kinds of boundaries

Try it

Watch the Atlantic open

Diagram

Evidence the continents fit together

Simplified shapes, not to scale. Real evidence: coastlines fit, the same fossils (the freshwater reptile Mesosaurus, the fern Glossopteris) appear on both sides of the ocean, matching rock types and mountain ranges, and glacier scratches that line up.

Data

How fast do plates move?

Typical speeds in centimeters per year. Your fingernails grow about 4 cm a year, as fast as many plates move. Over a million years that adds up to tens of kilometers.

Concept 3 · Earthquakes and volcanoes

What happens at the edges

Plates snag on each other, stress builds, then they suddenly slip: an earthquake. Where one plate sinks, rock melts and rises: a volcano. Most of both happen along plate boundaries.

Analogy

A stuck book, and a shaken soda

Stick and slip

Pull a book with a rubber band. It sticks, the band stretches, then it jerks. That jerk is an earthquake.

Shaken soda

Gas dissolved in magma expands as it rises and blasts out like opening a shaken soda.

Pushed rug

Push two edges of a rug together and it bunches into a ridge. Colliding plates do this to make mountains.

Try it

Build up stress, trigger a quake

Push again and again. Nobody knows exactly when it will slip.

Diagram

A subduction zone

The sinking plate drags water down. Water lowers the melting point of the hot rock above it, magma forms, and it rises. This is how the Pacific Ring of Fire gets its volcanoes.

Data

Big quakes are rare. Small ones are everywhere.

Approximate yearly worldwide counts (USGS-style rounded). Each whole step up in magnitude is about 10 times fewer quakes but about 32 times more energy released.

Concept 4 · The rock cycle

Rocks recycle

Rocks slowly change from one type to another: igneous (cooled magma), sedimentary (squeezed pieces), metamorphic (changed by heat and pressure). No rock is permanent.

Analogy

Crayons

Melt and cool = igneous

Melt a crayon and let it harden. Same idea as lava or magma cooling.

Shavings pressed = sedimentary

Pack crayon shavings in layers and press. Bits of old rock get squeezed into layers.

Warm and squish = metamorphic

Warm a crayon and squeeze it. It changes shape and swirl without melting. Pressure and heat change rocks without melting them.

Real rocks take thousands to millions of years; a crayon takes minutes.

Where it breaks: squeezed crayon shavings stick because wax is soft. Sedimentary rock is cemented by minerals over a long time, and metamorphic rock usually recrystallizes into new minerals instead of just bending.

Try it

Take a rock on a journey

Data

Concept 5 · Shaping the surface

Break, carry, drop

Weathering breaks rock into pieces, erosion carries the pieces away, and deposition drops them somewhere new. Water, wind, and ice do the work.

Analogy

A grater, a conveyor belt, and a dump truck

Three different jobs, often happening at once. Weathering is the grater: it breaks big rock into small pieces. Erosion is the conveyor belt: water, wind, or ice carries the pieces away. Deposition is the dump truck: the load stops moving and piles up. A river can do all three in one bend: it grinds rock, carries sand, and drops it on the inside bank.

Where it breaks: real erosion has no separate machines. One storm can weather, carry, and dump in the same hour.

Diagram

A bending river

The river slowly swings sideways as it carves one bank and builds the other.

Try it

Fast water vs. slow water

Simplified minimum speeds. Fast floods move boulders; slow lakes only settle clay. That is why the sediment in a delta is sorted by size.

Real world

Ever sinceWind, waves, and rain keep weathering and moving sediment.Sleeping Bear Dunes, Pictured Rocks cliffs, beach sand
Glacial leftoversBoulders dragged from far away and dropped as the ice melted.Big rounded boulders (erratics) in Ann Arbor yards and parks

Dates are approximate and rounded.

Build it

Engineering challenge: the riverbank guard

The problem: protect a sand riverbank from washing away when water is poured down the same slope that erodes an unprotected bank.

Criteria: less sand collects at the bottom than from the unprotected bank, using the same amount of water both times.

Constraints: rocks from the yard rock collection, sticks, or other small objects pressed into the sand. No glue or tape, and no reshaping the slope itself.

  1. Try it in the game first. Play Rock Cycle Router at the bottom of this page. Notice which moves are weathering and which are erosion.
  2. Plan. Sketch two different ideas on your design log. Label how each one slows the water down or blocks it from carrying sand away.
  3. Build and test. Pour the same amount of water down the unprotected bank first and collect the sand that washes off. Then test your protected bank the same way, with a clean collection cup.
  4. Improve. Change one thing, test again, and record it.

Print a design log for each team. This is the same problem as a real levee or breakwater: slow the water, and it drops its sediment instead of carrying it away.

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

Explain why Michigan has no volcanoes but lots of sand dunes and boulders, and how a rock could end up as marble.

Show a model answer

Michigan is in the middle of a plate, far from the boundaries where plates collide or pull apart, so there are no volcanoes and few earthquakes. Instead, its surface was reshaped by glaciers that ground up rock and carried boulders (weathering, erosion, deposition), and wind and waves still move sand into dunes.

Limestone is a sedimentary rock made of shells and mud pressed together. If heat and pressure from plate collisions change it without melting, it becomes marble, a metamorphic rock.

Words to know

crust
Earth's thin, rocky outer layer.
mantle
Thick layer of hot, slowly flowing rock under the crust.
core
Iron-nickel center: liquid outside, solid inside.
plate
A giant slab of crust and upper mantle.
boundary
Where two plates meet.
earthquake
Shaking when plates suddenly slip.
magma
Molten rock underground. It is called lava on the surface.
igneous rock
Formed from cooled magma or lava.
sedimentary rock
Formed from squeezed layers of sediment.
metamorphic rock
Changed by heat and pressure without melting.
weathering
Breaking rock into smaller pieces.
erosion
Moving broken pieces from place to place.
deposition
Dropping the carried pieces.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $10): a hard-boiled egg, modeling clay in layers, crayons and a grater, a toaster or warm water bath (adult-supervised) for melting, graham crackers and frosting, sandpaper, a stream table made from a baking tray with sand, a rock collection from the yard.

  • Concept 1: crack a hard-boiled egg: shell = crust, white = mantle, yolk = core. Cut a layered clay ball in half.
  • Concept 2: push graham crackers on frosting: apart (divergent), together (convergent), sideways (transform).
  • Concept 3: pull a rubber-banded book across a table until it jerks. Shake and open a soda outdoors.
  • Concept 4: grate crayon shavings, press and warm gently between wax paper; melt a crayon to compare.
  • Concept 5: tilt a tray of sand and pour water at different speeds. Sort the deposits by size. Then run the riverbank guard challenge (about 30 to 40 minutes), reusing the stream table and rock collection already in the kit.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Earth's mantle is liquid." It's solid rock that flows very slowly.
  • "Continents float on water." They are parts of plates riding on hot, soft rock.
  • "Metamorphic rocks are melted." If melted, they'd become igneous.
  • "Earthquakes can be predicted exactly." We know where, not exactly when.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions.
